Nevertheless, he establishes the middle clause as a case where the injured party is uncertain, and Tosafot's explanation requires that, because there is partial admission, Sumchus would require division. Likewise, Tosafot's necessity analysis in s.v. ra'ui, which applies according to all opinions, must mean that even according to the view that Sumchus does not apply where both parties are certain, the rule of division applies in a case of partial admission where the injured party is uncertain and the tortfeasor is certain. If that is so, all the more so where the injured party also makes a definite claim. A definite claim by the injured party is stronger than an uncertain claim. It would therefore follow that where there is partial admission, everyone agrees that Sumchus requires division even when both parties are certain. But this is difficult from Bava Metzia 100. The Gemara there asks from the Mishnah: one says that he sold the larger slave and the other says the smaller, and the defendant must swear. This is understandable according to the view that Sumchus does not apply where both parties are certain, for then he swears. But according to the view that Sumchus applies even where both are certain, why should he swear? They should divide. Yet that very Mishnah involves partial admission, as indicated by the obligation to swear. According to the reasoning above, Sumchus should require division there according to all opinions, even according to the view that he does not ordinarily apply his rule to two definite claims. The Gemara's question should therefore arise according to everyone, even before it knows the answer that Sumchus agrees where there is a Torah oath. It is difficult to answer that the questioner certainly anticipated the Gemara's eventual answer that Sumchus agrees where a Torah oath exists, but nevertheless reasoned that if the claimant protests, "What do I care about your oath? Give me half under Sumchus's rule," we should listen to him. He could argue that if the defendant had denied everything, the claimant would have received half, so why should the claimant's position be weakened and he lose everything merely because the defendant admitted a small part? Perhaps the defendant is strategically admitting a perutah in order to escape division. The questioner would then be understood as saying that they should divide, while the answer would be that in any event, once the Torah imposes an oath, Sumchus's division rule does not apply. If the claimant had demanded an oath rather than division, the defendant would have had to swear. Conversely, when the claimant seeks division, the defendant may say, "I am prepared to swear, and we shall accept whichever result the Torah gives." This might explain why the question is raised only according to the view that Sumchus applies to two definite claims even in total denial. According to the view that Sumchus does not apply except where there is partial admission, the possibility of strategic partial admission creates no difficulty, for if the defendant denied everything he would owe nothing in a case of two definite claims. Still, this entire explanation is strained. It therefore appears that a recognized rule is decisive here: a migo that would require brazenness is not accepted to exempt one from an oath, but it is accepted with respect to monetary liability, as I discussed at length above in the rules of migo. This is almost unanimously accepted by the authorities. Accordingly, consider the case discussed above where the injured party says he is uncertain and the tortfeasor says he is certain. If the tortfeasor totally denied liability, Sumchus would not require division, but where he partially admits liability Tosafot say that Sumchus does require division. This seems difficult because the tortfeasor has a migo that he could have denied everything. He is therefore like one who returns a lost item voluntarily. One might answer, following Rabbah's explanation of why the Torah imposes an oath on one who partially admits a claim, that a person generally does not have the brazenness to deny the entire claim. But that answer works only if we seek to exempt him from an oath. Here we seek to exempt him from monetary liability, and with respect to money we do accept even a migo that involves brazenness. We must therefore say that the Mishnah concerns a case where witnesses saw the goring but did not know whether the larger or smaller ox caused it. The tortfeasor then has no migo to deny everything, because he cannot contradict the witnesses. Where there are no witnesses, everyone agrees that even in a case of partial admission Sumchus does not require division, because the tortfeasor has a migo that he could have denied everything, and with respect to money we disregard the brazenness involved. Accordingly, all the Mishnayot cited above are resolved. Those Mishnayot do not concern cases supported by witnesses. Sumchus therefore agrees that the burden of proof rests upon the claimant, and this is why they teach complete exemption. The Gemara's question is also precise. According to the view that Sumchus does not apply where both parties make definite claims and the defendant totally denies liability, there is no question that they should divide. Even if the defendant partially admits, he has a migo that he could have denied everything, and since Sumchus does not apply in two definite claims with total denial, that migo defeats division. This applies in the absence of witnesses. Even though Rav Pappa holds that half damages are compensatory, so that it is not necessary to say that the Mishnah specifically deals with witnesses, the Mishnah is stated without qualification and includes both a case where witnesses exist and one where they do not. It is therefore necessary to teach the Sages' position against Sumchus in the case where witnesses do exist. Sumchus would require division there, and the Mishnah teaches that even there the Sages say that the burden of proof rests upon the claimant. This properly explains the matter. According to Rabbenu Yerucham's understanding, the sugya can therefore be read as follows, even according to Rav Pappa. One cannot answer simply that the tortfeasor stands by his statement. Since the first clause involves two definite claims, the latter clause should likewise involve two definite claims. If so, why are both clauses necessary? We might answer that the first teaches the strength of Sumchus's rule, that even with two definite claims they divide, while the second teaches the strength of the Sages, that even with partial admission they disagree and require proof. But that would itself be obvious, because in the absence of witnesses the tortfeasor has a migo to deny everything. If the Sages reject Sumchus in the first clause, then certainly they reject him in the latter clause. Conversely, if Sumchus requires division in a case of partial admission even though the defendant could totally deny, then he must also apply his rule where there is total denial. The two clauses would again be redundant. If we say that witnesses exist, so that the defendant cannot deny everything, then the case should constitute a refutation of Rabbah bar Natan. The claimant's assertion of wheat is an admission that rejects the witnesses concerning barley. If so, once the witnesses are rejected by his admission, the tortfeasor could again deny the barley entirely, and the migo problem returns. Thus both clauses would remain unnecessary. If the middle clause instead concerns a definite claim by the injured party and uncertainty by the tortfeasor, the wording "No, rather" becomes difficult. Tosafot therefore explain that even if the first clause includes a case of definite claims and the latter clause a case of uncertainty, the first may still have been stated alongside the second. But then the comparison to Sumchus does not work unless the latter clause, because of its partial admission, is a case in which Sumchus applies even where both parties make definite claims. That makes the phrase "No, rather" meaningful, and the first clause is then taught incidentally because of the second. The Gemara can consequently challenge Rabbah bar Natan precisely. Since the defendant has a migo to deny everything, and if witnesses exist the claimant's own admission has rejected those witnesses, how can the partial admission generate a different result? The Gemara therefore establishes the case as one where the injured party is uncertain and the tortfeasor is certain. The phrase "No, rather" is then precise, and the first clause is taught incidentally because of the second even though Sumchus does not apply to the first in exactly the same manner. This resolves the matter. Examine it carefully, for the reasoning is subtle. All of this follows the version that reads Rav Pappa in the sugya. From the Rosh's words, however, it appears that he did not have the reading of Rav Pappa and understood the entire discussion as following the opinion that half damages are a fine. According to that version the matter is, in any event, readily explained as stated above. This, at least, provides a clear and correct explanation of Rabbenu Yerucham. There is in fact support for Rabbenu Yerucham's understanding that the Rosh does not identify admission with waiver. In chapter 2 of Ketubot the Rosh discusses one who says, "This promissory note is a note of accommodation." Where this statement causes a loss to others, he is not believed. The Rosh asks why he is not believed through a migo that he could simply waive the debt. He answers that the creditor does not wish to lose the debt. If he waived it, the borrower would no longer have to pay him, whereas by saying that the note is merely a note of accommodation he knows that the borrower is not a robber. This is difficult. Even now, by saying that the note is fictitious and admitting that he never lent the money, his statement should itself amount to a waiver. The borrower would therefore still not be a robber. What difference is there between admitting that no barley was lent and admitting that the loan represented by this promissory note never occurred? I see no distinction. It is strained to say that there his admission was made only to keep the debt away from his own creditors and is therefore not a complete admission. If so, the same should apply to an ostensible waiver, for in his heart he does not intend to waive. It is difficult to distinguish between them. Nevertheless, the plain implication of the Tur is that he does not accept Rabbenu Yerucham's view. If he did, he should have stated that where the defendant stands by his admission, he must pay. How could the Tur omit such a significant law, especially if, as explained above, there is a distinction between a case with witnesses and a case where the defendant himself continues to stand by his admission? There is also a difficulty in the Rosh himself. If there is a genuine distinction between admission and waiver, why did he depart from Rashi and Tosafot, who explain the exemption as resulting from waiver? His objection was that it happens every day that a person has several claims and demands only one of them. But the Rosh could have answered Rashi exactly as he answers for himself, namely that the case is one where the two claims arose at the same time and in the same transaction. In that circumstance, by failing to claim both at once, the claimant has waived the second, just as the Rosh says that his omission constitutes an admission. Why then reject Rashi's explanation at all? Rather, it is clear that the two concepts are really one. The claimant's admission operates because it is treated as waiver. This is why a litigant's admission is equivalent to one hundred witnesses, because through his admission he relinquishes his right, as explained above in siman 75 and in my discussion of the admission of Issur the convert. Indeed, waiver is the stronger and more natural concept here. If the reason were only admission, it could apply even to a deposit, just like Issur's admission, whereas pure waiver is more difficult to apply to property that remains legally in the depositor's possession, as I wrote above. Rashi too certainly agrees that the claimant's failure to demand the barley is treated as an admission, just as the Rosh says regarding the Mishnah in HaManiach, where waiver does not naturally apply and the operative idea is admission. The difference is only that Rashi understood the general statement, "he claimed wheat and admitted barley," to apply even where the two alleged debts did not arise at the same time. As Maharshal writes, in such a case there is no inference from the fact that the claimant did not demand barley, because a person does not necessarily demand all his separate claims at once. Rashi therefore explains the waiver differently. Since the defendant admitted barley and the claimant did not immediately respond, within the time required for speech, "You also owe me barley," his silence demonstrates that he waived the barley. The Rosh objects that there is no such proof. Since a person need not pursue all his claims at once, there was no reason for the claimant to say anything about the barley when he was not presently demanding it. The Rosh therefore concludes that the case must involve claims arising at the same time and in the same transaction. Once we reach that conclusion, there is no need to describe the result as an independent waiver. The claimant's omission itself is an admission, exactly as in the case of one ox pursuing another. But in truth, where both liabilities arose at the same time, there is no practical distinction between admission and waiver. On the contrary, the concepts reinforce each other. There is further proof from Bava Metzia in the sugya of the borrowed and rented animals. Ramban sought to compare that case to one who claims wheat and the defendant admits barley. The Rosh rejects the comparison and writes: in the case of wheat and barley, the claimant waived the barley, as Rashi explains in chapter HaManiach, etc. He concludes there that because the claimant did not claim the barley, he waived it or admitted that no barley was owed. Had the Rosh disagreed with Rashi's concept of waiver, there would have been no reason for him to cite Rashi's explanation. The Rosh's formulation, "he waived it or admitted that it was not owed," likewise shows that, as a matter of law where the claims arise at the same time, there is no difference between the two formulations. They are two descriptions of the same legal effect. This is especially compelling against Rabbenu Yerucham's rule that if the defendant stands by his admission, the rule of wheat and barley no longer applies. In the case of the borrowed and rented animals the renter unquestionably stands by his statement that the rented animal died in the ordinary manner. Yet Ramban applies the wheat and barley principle, and the Rosh discusses the comparison without saying that continued adherence to the admission removes the exemption. It is therefore clear that Rabbenu Yerucham's qualification is not correct. The Rosh's own words, which the later authorities did not cite in this connection, explicitly show that even an admission is treated as waiver for purposes of this law.

And at a particular time, etc. This is the view of the Rosh. Maharshal, in Yam Shel Shlomo, writes that the formulation is stated without qualification and therefore implies that the rule applies even if the two loans did not occur on the same day. Addressing the Rosh's difficulty, he explains that after the defendant admitted the barley, the claimant returned to demanding wheat and did not mention barley in his renewed claim. This demonstrates that he waived the barley. The Shach writes that even the Rosh agrees with this rule where the circumstances are as Maharshal describes, namely that the claimant returned and again demanded wheat. Even if the two loans did not arise together, he is then exempt from the barley. The Rosh merely found it strained to interpret Rabbah bar Natan's statement in this manner, especially since the Rosh raised another difficulty against Rashi's explanation based on waiver. See there. In my opinion, Tosafot provide proof for Maharshal's view. Moreover, even the Rosh, who explains the rule in terms of admission, means that the admission occurs only when the claimant returns and again demands the wheat, not beforehand. Nevertheless, the Rosh still does not accept that this is a waiver where the two loans did not arise together, because the fact that the claimant returned to demand wheat proves nothing about the separate barley debt. Since the two debts did not arise together, he had no reason to concern himself with demanding the other one at that time. My difficulty is with Tosafot, s.v. leima, who ask why the Mishnah could not follow Rabban Gamliel, who holds that where one claims wheat and the defendant admits barley, the defendant is liable. Tosafot answer that even Rabban Gamliel agrees that the defendant is exempt from paying the barley itself. Rabban Gamliel holds only that the admission nevertheless creates an oath of partial admission. See there. I do not understand this. Suppose a claimant says to another, "You owe me one hundred gold coins. Fifty are waived to you, and pay me the other fifty," and the defendant responds, "I never owed you except fifty, and those fifty are waived by you." Could one imagine that the defendant is liable for an oath of partial admission? He has admitted owing nothing that remains payable. There could be no clearer case of total denial. It therefore appears that Tosafot agree with Maharshal. On the claimant's first demand there is not yet any waiver, because a person does not necessarily demand all his claims at once. Only after the defendant admits barley and the claimant then returns to demand wheat does the principal waiver occur. Accordingly, at the moment when the defendant admitted the barley, his statement was still a complete and effective monetary admission. Had the claimant not returned to his original demand, the defendant would have been liable for the barley. That initial admission is therefore sufficient to create the status of partial admission and the accompanying oath. This is clear. The same must be said in the Rosh. In his criticism of the Rif, who holds that seizure does not help with respect to the barley, the Rosh writes that the claimant cannot retain the value of the wheat, because the defendant denies that obligation and seizure in the presence of witnesses does not help. The defendant is exempt upon taking an oath according to Rabban Gamliel, and according to the Sages even without an oath. As for the barley, seizure does not help because the claimant has already admitted that it was not owed or has waived it. These are his words. The Rosh clearly assumes that everyone agrees that the barley itself is exempt, while he makes the obligation to swear depend upon the dispute between Rabban Gamliel and the Sages. Thus, according to Rabban Gamliel, there remains an oath of partial admission. The difficulty just stated therefore applies equally to the Rosh. We must consequently say that according to the Rosh as well, the decisive admission by the claimant occurs only when he subsequently reiterates his demand for wheat. Before that renewed demand, there was no admission. At the time the defendant first admitted barley, therefore, he made a genuine monetary admission. His statement constituted partial admission for purposes of Rabban Gamliel's oath. It follows, however, that the Rosh must hold that where the two debts did not arise at the same time, the claimant's renewed demand of wheat still does not amount to an admission concerning the barley. The Shach's proof from Rabbenu Yerucham is not compelling, because Rabbenu Yerucham speaks of a claimant who says, "No, rather it was wheat." The expression "No, rather" leaves no room for doubt that he rejects the barley entirely and thereby relinquishes any other claim, for he explicitly says "No." But where the claimant merely repeats his original demand without that formulation, even after the defendant has mentioned barley, one may still say that he simply chose not to demand a separate loan that arose at another time, for whatever reason.

And one should not infer against the Rosh that, in any event, this oath itself is difficult. The claimant has seized the barley, so the amount admitted is already in his hands and would seem to be heilech, since the very money corresponding to the defendant's admission is already possessed by the claimant. One may answer that according to the reasoning the Rosh was discussing, seizure works because of a whichever way you look at it argument: either give me the barley, or I will retain what I seized toward the value of the wheat. On that theory, even seizure after the parties have already appeared in judgment is effective. It therefore is not heilech, because at the time of the defendant's admission the admitted amount was not yet in the claimant's hands. This is straightforward. Nor should one argue that the Rosh could have proven his position more simply. If claiming wheat and admitting barley referred to a barley loan made at another time, and the claimant's failure to demand that barley loan constituted waiver, then the same should be true even where he claimed wheat lent in Nisan and the defendant admitted wheat lent in Tishrei. The defendant should be exempt because the claimant did not demand the Tishrei loan and therefore evidently waived it. One may answer that the Rosh writes in the sugya of the borrowed and rented animals that people do not confuse wheat with barley. By contrast, they may confuse times. The claimant may confuse Tishrei with Nisan. Accordingly, where both claims concern wheat, the defendant can say that the loan he admits is the very loan being claimed, except that the claimant erred regarding the date. This resolves the point. Still, according to what I wrote, one could say that even when the barley itself is exempt, an oath may remain because the defendant made a partial admission, while the Sages exempt him from the oath only because they hold that the admission must be of the same kind as the claim. If so, where both claims concern wheat, the admission is certainly of the same kind as the claim and the defendant would not be exempt from an oath. Rabbah bar Natan, however, states a complete exemption. Yet this is not a sufficient answer either, because if the defendant admitted the same quantity of wheat that the claimant demanded, there is no denied amount at all. What partial admission would there be upon which to impose an oath?

And if he seized it. This is the view of the Rif and Rambam. The Rosh, however, asks according to his approach that if so, the Gemara should also have established the middle clause as a case of seizure rather than as one where the injured party says he is uncertain and the tortfeasor says he is certain. The Shach writes to resolve this. Before considering his resolution, however, we must understand the Rosh's question itself. Why does the Rosh not ask the same question against his own approach? Let both clauses be established as cases where the injured party is uncertain and the tortfeasor is certain. One must answer, as Rashi and Tosafot do, that if so the two clauses would be redundant. But if the Rif's explanation is that both clauses concern seizure, the same redundancy exists. It is true that the Rosh was careful on this point and wrote that the middle clause should have been established as a case of seizure and the final clause as a case of a definite claim against an uncertain one. Yet the need for this is unclear. What do we gain? The difficulty against Rabbah bar Mamal that the Mishnah does not deal with two definite claims remains. Surely the first, middle, and final clauses are all meant to parallel one another. As the Gemara itself explains, the final clause involves the injured party making a definite claim, the tortfeasor being uncertain, and seizure, while the middle clause has the reverse, the tortfeasor certain and the injured party uncertain, and the first clause again has the tortfeasor uncertain and the injured party certain. All the clauses thus contain some combination of definite and uncertain claims. If we reverse the explanations, the clauses are still parallel. The final clause would have the injured party uncertain and the tortfeasor certain, while the middle and first clauses would have the injured party certain and the tortfeasor uncertain, with the middle clause involving seizure. What, then, has been gained? The original difficulty remains. The Maadanei Melech apparently seeks to resolve this by saying that the way of the Gemara is to give the more comfortable explanation first and only afterward resort to a strained one. Thus, on the first difficulty the Gemara should have answered with seizure. This is not sufficient, especially as a basis for rejecting the Rif. Who can weigh the Gemara's answers so precisely as to say that the explanation involving uncertainty by the injured party is more comfortable than the explanation involving seizure? Seizure is itself entirely unmentioned in the Mishnah. It therefore appears that the Rosh follows the view of the Nimukei Yosef regarding the case where the claimant says that the larger mu'ad ox caused the damage and the other says that the smaller mu'ad ox caused it. Both obligations are paid from the owner's superior assets, and therefore the admission is of the same kind as the claim. It is comparable to one who claims one hundred as a loan and the defendant admits fifty. If so, the final clause necessarily concerns either an injured party who is uncertain or a tortfeasor who is uncertain. Otherwise, how could the Mishnah merely say that the burden of proof rests upon the claimant in the case where the claimant says the larger mu'ad caused the damage and the other says the smaller mu'ad caused it? The defendant would be liable for a Torah oath, and the Mishnah should have said that he must swear. Moreover, what would the Mishnah teach against Sumchus? Sumchus agrees that his division rule does not apply where a Torah oath exists, as explained above. We must therefore say either that the injured party is uncertain, in which case there is no definite claim upon which to impose an oath, or that the tortfeasor is uncertain. In the latter case the rule that one who cannot swear must pay does not apply because the tortfeasor had no reason to know which ox caused the damage, as the Shach writes below in siman 400. If so, why did Rav Pappa need all the lengthy analysis involving a supposed refutation of Rabbah bar Natan and the like? He could have asked much more simply: the final clause necessarily involves one party being uncertain. Therefore the middle and first clauses must also involve a definite and uncertain claim, whether the injured party or the tortfeasor is the uncertain one. They cannot be cases of two definite claims. We must consequently say that the required parallelism is primarily between the first and middle clauses, not between those clauses and the final clause. The Rosh's question is therefore sound. The Gemara could have established the first and middle clauses as cases of two definite claims together with seizure, while allowing the final clause to involve a definite and uncertain claim, since no full parallelism to the final clause is required. There is, however, another point. Tosafot write according to the view that one who says, "Fifty I know and fifty I do not know," is exempt, that even in a case of partial admission, why should he swear if he has a migo that he could have said concerning the denied portion, "I do not know"? They answer that a person does not willingly say, "I do not know," because that makes him appear dishonest. According to this, in a case of goring, where a person who says he does not know whether the larger or smaller ox caused the damage is not subject to the rule that one who cannot swear must pay because he had no reason to know, even one who says definitely that the smaller ox caused the damage should be exempt from an oath. He has a migo that he could say, "I do not know," and Tosafot's answer does not apply because such uncertainty would not make him appear dishonest in a matter he had no reason to know. If so, there may be no oath here at all. This also helps explain the Rif. The Rosh properly asks that the middle clause should have been established as a case of seizure rather than the final clause. At first glance, what is the question? Even if we say that the final clause involves a definite claim against uncertainty, the final clause also includes two definite claims because the Mishnah says, "No, rather," and in the case where the claimant says that the larger mu'ad caused the damage while the other says the smaller mu'ad caused it, an oath should be required. We would therefore still need seizure, since according to the authorities a pledge or property already in hand is heilech. Yet one may answer that there is no oath here because the defendant has a migo that he could have said he does not know, as just explained. But the Rif holds that a migo is not accepted to exempt one from an oath. If so, according to the Rif seizure is indeed required in the final clause, and the Rosh's question falls away. Examine this carefully. The same must be said concerning Tosafot there, s.v. leima. They ask why the Mishnah could not follow Rabban Gamliel, who obligates an oath where one claims wheat and the defendant admits barley. But then why does the Mishnah say only that the burden of proof rests upon the claimant? It should say that the defendant must swear. Also, Sumchus does not disagree where there is a Torah oath. We must therefore say that Tosafot regard the defendant's admission concerning the tam ox as heilech, because the injured party is already a partner in that ox and may consecrate his share. It is therefore comparable to a deposit already available to the claimant, contrary to the Shach's position below in siman 400. The Shach brings a proof from Tosafot at the beginning of chapter HaParah. Tosafot ask why, even where the injured party makes a definite claim and the tortfeasor is uncertain, we do not apply the rule that one who cannot swear must pay. They answer either that the tortfeasor had no reason to know or that an admission to a fine exempts him. Tosafot do not answer that the admission is heilech. This is no proof. Tosafot's first answer itself is difficult to understand. Why did the question arise at all? It is obvious that there can be no oath where, if the defendant admitted liability, he would be exempt as one who admits a fine. Rather, Tosafot's first answer must understand the Mishnah's general formulation to include even a mu'ad ox. In that case the rule that one who cannot swear must pay does apply, and there is no concept of heilech because payment from a mu'ad is taken from superior assets rather than from the body of the ox. In Tosafot's second answer, which establishes the case as one involving a tam, there is no need to invoke heilech because there is no oath at all, since an admission to the fine would exempt him. Moreover, according to one establishment in Shevuot, Shmuel holds that where one claims wheat and barley and the defendant admits one of them, he is exempt from an oath, while heilech itself creates liability according to Rabbenu Tam, as Tosafot write in Bava Metzia 5, s.v. i nami. Yet Shmuel himself is the one who says that the rule applies even where the injured party makes a definite claim, etc. Tosafot therefore needed an answer to Shmuel's statement that works according to every establishment. They could not rely on heilech, since according to Shmuel heilech may obligate rather than exempt. There is thus no proof from that passage. Here, however, the sugya does indicate that Tosafot's answer depends upon treating the tam ox as heilech. There remains a difficulty regarding the middle and final clauses. In the final clause, where the claimant says the larger mu'ad ox caused the damage and the defendant says the smaller mu'ad did, even if we disagree with the Nimukei Yosef, it is impossible to say that the Mishnah follows Rabban Gamliel unless we say that an oath is required, because there is no heilech with respect to a mu'ad. We must therefore say that Tosafot agree with the Nimukei Yosef that this is an admission of the same kind as the claim. If so, the final clause independently must involve one party being uncertain. Yet Rav Pappa does not derive his argument from that clause. This shows that parallelism to the final clause is not essential. Tosafot's question is therefore sound: perhaps the Mishnah follows Rabban Gamliel, while the middle clause involves heilech. In that case, however, what room is there for the Rosh's question against the Rif, who does not accept the Nimukei Yosef's view, as I will explain below in siman 400, and Rambam likewise does not accept it? According to the Rif, full parallelism throughout the Mishnah can indeed be required, and the objection disappears. There is another possible resolution. Rav Pappa does not establish the middle clause as involving seizure because it is certainly strained to interpret a Mishnah that says only that the claimant must bring proof as secretly referring to property already seized by the claimant. Seizure is not mentioned at all. But if, independently, we must say that even though the Mishnah says that the burden of proof rests upon the claimant it nevertheless concerns a case where the injured party had seized the ox, then it is reasonable to say that the seizure occurred from the outset before the claims were made. Once we already know that the Mishnah deals with seizure, we can use that fact throughout. This is relevant according to the view that half damages are a fine. The Rosh asks how the Mishnah can involve the owner's admission, since even if he admitted every detail he would be exempt as one who admits a fine. The Rosh's answer, that there were witnesses but they did not know which ox gored, is strained, like the Gemara's question in Bava Batra: if there are witnesses, let us see what they say. Here too, the difficulty is obvious. The Maggid Mishneh therefore explains that the injured party had seized the ox. Seizure prevents the tortfeasor's admission from exempting him from half damages even according to the view that half damages are a fine. Once the Mishnah must in any event be understood as involving seizure, it is reasonable to say that the injured party seized before making his claim, and then the rule of claiming wheat and admitting barley does not apply. Accordingly, the Rif may hold that the anonymous Gemara, which follows the ruling that half damages are a fine, answers with seizure, and that answer in truth applies to the middle clause as well. The Gemara does not ask from the middle clause because it could have answered that the injured party is fit to take there and has nothing, since no baraita was cited to contradict such an explanation, as I wrote above. But in substance the seizure answer can apply there too. Rav Pappa, by contrast, holds that half damages are compensatory and therefore has no independent reason to introduce seizure into the Mishnah. For him, seizure remains unmentioned and strained, so he cannot use that answer. He therefore establishes the middle clause as one where the injured party is uncertain. The same applies to the final clause. The Rif need not accept Rashi and Tosafot's claim that the clauses would then be redundant, because many distinctions make each clause necessary, as Tosafot themselves discuss. The anonymous Gemara that answers with seizure follows Rabbah bar Mamal and, as explained, can maintain that Sumchus applies even to two definite claims. The entire Mishnah can therefore remain a case of two definite claims. Everything is properly explained.

And there is a clear proof for the Rif that the seizure explanation applies to the first clause as well. We must explain Rav Pappa's establishment of the middle clause as one where the injured party is uncertain and the tortfeasor is certain, and the first clause in the reverse, with the injured party certain and the tortfeasor uncertain. Although the Mishnah says "No, rather," which ordinarily indicates two definite claims, Tosafot and Maharsha explain that the clause includes such a case but that Sumchus's disagreement is relevant only to the case of uncertainty. At first glance, why was Rav Pappa forced to make the first and middle clauses only imperfectly parallel, with uncertainty on opposite sides? It would seem simpler to establish both as cases where both parties are uncertain. In such a case Sumchus and the Sages disagree directly. It is true that the middle clause also includes the case where the injured party is uncertain and the tortfeasor is certain, which explains the words "No, rather," but there would then be no novelty in saying that Sumchus does not require division in that subcase. One could hardly say that the entire first clause is superfluous, because if it comes merely to teach that Sumchus requires division where both are uncertain, many Mishnayot already establish that rule, such as the beginning of chapter HaParah and the Mishnayot concerning the borrowed and rented animals and concerning an exchange. Nor is it necessary to teach that the Sages disagree even there. If, in the middle clause where there is partial admission, the Sages nevertheless say that the burden of proof rests upon the claimant, then all the more so in the first clause where the defendant totally denies liability. We must therefore say that the first clause concerns an injured party making a definite claim and a tortfeasor who is uncertain. It teaches that even there the Sages apply the rule that the burden of proof rests upon the claimant, contrary to Sumchus. The middle clause must correspondingly be understood in that way as well to the extent the wording allows, which is strained, as Maharsha notes. Were it not for the implication of "No, rather," we would have established the whole matter as uncertainty on both sides. There is, however, a way to explain the wording. In the first clause, although the main dispute between Sumchus and the Sages concerns the case where the injured party is certain and the tortfeasor uncertain, the Mishnah still says "No, rather" because it also includes two definite claims. It teaches that even where the ox was a mu'ad that was pursuing the injured animal, the Sages nevertheless allow the tortfeasor to say that the animal was struck by a rock, as Rambam rules, contrary to the view of Maharshal. The Mishnah says simply "an ox," which includes a mu'ad. But in the middle clause, if the actual dispute were only where both parties were uncertain, why would the Mishnah say "No, rather" merely to include an additional case where the injured party is uncertain and the tortfeasor certain? There would be no practical dispute in that additional case, since Sumchus too would agree that the possessor's definite claim prevails. The phrase would teach nothing. Therefore the middle clause itself must involve a case where the injured party is uncertain and the tortfeasor certain, and even there Sumchus requires division while the Sages apply the rule that the burden of proof rests upon the claimant. If so, the final clause likewise necessarily involves the injured party uncertain and the tortfeasor certain, at least according to Rabbah bar Mamal, who maintains that the first clause involves two definite claims and whose approach still requires the middle clause to have the tortfeasor making a definite claim in order for the wording to be meaningful. But this creates a major difficulty according to Abaye. Tosafot in Bava Batra 135, s.v. Abaye, write that Abaye holds that even where the uncertain party had absolutely no reason to know, a definite claim is still superior. How then can the first clause, where the injured party is certain and the tortfeasor uncertain, conclude according to the Sages that the burden of proof rests upon the claimant? The claimant's definite claim should prevail. All the more so in the middle clause, where the injured party is uncertain and the tortfeasor certain, why should Sumchus require division? Tosafot's answer that the uncertain party had no reason to know does not work according to Abaye. This is a powerful difficulty. The Rif therefore must hold as I have written, that once the Gemara introduces seizure, that answer applies to the middle clause as well and the clauses can be understood as cases of two definite claims. Abaye can explain the middle clause as two definite claims, where Sumchus and the Sages disagree, without any difficulty from the principle that a definite claim is superior to an uncertain one. The rule of seizure also removes the difficulty from Rabbah bar Natan. Thus the Rif's interpretation is necessary for Abaye according to the view attributed to him by Tosafot in Bava Batra. This is, in my opinion, a clear and powerful proof for the Rif. Tosafot in HaManiach, who do not apply seizure to the first and middle clauses, follow their own view in chapter HaParah that even Abaye agrees that where the uncertain party had no reason to know, a definite claim is not superior. They therefore face no difficulty. The Rif, however, follows the other approach recorded by Tosafot in Bava Batra, as explained above, and his position has a clear proof.

The value of the barley. The Sema writes that the reason is that since the claimant is already in possession, he can say, "I neither admitted nor waived the barley. I merely did not wish to demand everything at once." These are his words. At first glance they are incomprehensible. According to the Rama, seizure helps specifically if it occurred before the admission, but not afterward. If the Sema's reasoning were correct, seizure afterward should also help, because the claimant could say, "I know that I did not waive it." One cannot answer that this would be seizure after the doubt arose, because where the possessor makes a definite claim, seizure is effective even after the doubt arose, as the Rosh writes in Ketubot and Bava Metzia. See what I wrote above in the rules of seizure. This is particularly so according to the Mechaber, who holds that seizure even after the doubt arises is effective. We must therefore say that the Sema's reason was written only according to the opinion that seizure is effective even afterward, not according to those who distinguish based on the timing of seizure. Yet the Sema himself, in seif katan 26, cites the Nimukei Yosef's view distinguishing between seizure before the claimant's retraction and seizure afterward. His words therefore remain difficult. The Tur explicitly gives a different reason. He writes: since the claimant seized the barley, his failure to demand it is not considered an admission, because he can say, "I did not demand the barley because I was already in possession of it." This is a different explanation from the Sema's. Still, even the Rosh requires explanation. According to his own view, seizure helps only in the case of the two oxen. He writes: therefore, if the injured party seized before coming to beit din, even in the presence of witnesses, he collects according to what the tortfeasor says. Why does the Rosh require seizure specifically before coming to beit din? In the case of the two injured animals, the explanation that "I did not demand the smaller one because I was already in possession of it" seems inapplicable. The injured party cannot truthfully mean to demand both the large and the small ox, because the two claims are mutually exclusive. If the larger ox caused the damage, the smaller did not. Once he asserts in beit din that the larger ox caused the damage, he can no longer say that the smaller ox did. One might answer that this reason is needed only where the claimant could have claims regarding both items, whereas where the claims are mutually exclusive no such reason is necessary. But if so, the Rosh's objection to the Rif would fail. With wheat and barley it is possible that both claims are true, whereas with one large and one small ox both claims cannot be true. What then does seizure help there, since the Tur's explanation cannot apply? It is strained to say that the injured party could have come to beit din and said explicitly, "In my view the larger ox caused the damage, but if it is established otherwise, or if the owner admits only the smaller ox, then at least give me the value of the smaller." Such a formulation indeed would avoid both admission and waiver. If the claimant had seized, it could be treated as though he had made that reservation, because according to the Rosh both oxen are in his hands, while according to the Rif at least the smaller one is in his hands. This also resolves another difficulty in the Tur and Shulchan Aruch. They state generally that seizure helps. That is understandable if, according to the claimant, there were two separate loans, one of wheat and one of barley, even if they occurred on the same day and at the same hour. But what if, according to both parties, there was only one loan, and they disagree whether it was wheat or barley? The defendant is exempt, exactly like the case of one large and one small ox. In such a case seizure should seemingly not help even according to the Rif. The claimant cannot say, "Because I had already seized the barley I did not demand it," for he did demand this very loan and admitted by his formulation that it was not barley. According to what I have written, however, the matter is resolved. Seizure is treated as though the claimant had expressly reserved his rights by saying, "I am certain it was wheat, but if in fact it was barley, I do not waive or admit away that claim." Such a reservation works in every case. Yet even if we can interpret the Tur and Shulchan Aruch in this way according to the Rif, it is difficult to explain the Rosh this way because he grounds the rule in the claimant's admission. What reservation can overcome an express admission that the smaller ox did not damage the larger animal? Unless we say that the ultimate effect of such an admission is waiver, so that seizure is treated as though the claimant expressly stipulated that he does not waive. This itself is proof against the Shach's explanation of the Rosh above. All of this is strained if we distinguish between situations where the claimant could have claims against both items and situations where he could not. The same reasoning should apply even where the claims are mutually exclusive. There is also a difficulty in Tosafot. At the beginning of chapter HaParah, Tosafot ask according to Rashbam's view that Sumchus did not state his division rule where both parties make definite claims except when the disputed property stands in a neutral place, whereas when it is in the possessor's house Sumchus agrees that the burden of proof rests upon the claimant. If so, why did Rabbah bar Mamal feel compelled to say that the Mishnah does not follow Sumchus? Let the Mishnah follow Sumchus and concern a case where the tortfeasor's ox remained in the tortfeasor's house, in which case Sumchus agrees that the burden of proof rests upon the claimant. Yam Shel Shlomo discusses this question at length and treats it as a strong argument against Rashbam. But how can the Mishnah be explained that way? In the final clause involving the two injured animals, the difficulty from Rabbah bar Natan's rule of claiming wheat and admitting barley would remain. We would then have to say that the injured party seized both oxen, as the Rosh writes, and that the seizure occurred before he came to beit din. But if the ox is in the injured party's house, that is stronger possession than if it stood in a neutral field. Surely his position should not become weaker merely because he brought it into his own house. According to Sumchus, the Mishnah should therefore require division rather than simply apply the burden of proof to the claimant. The result could not be that the injured party either takes according to the tortfeasor or takes nothing where he did not seize, while if he did seize they divide. How then can the Mishnah simply state that the burden of proof rests upon the claimant, implying that with proof he takes according to the tortfeasor's admission? It follows that the Mishnah cannot follow Sumchus and must follow the Sages. According to the Sages, the Mishnah must be teaching their rule specifically against Sumchus, and therefore we establish the case as one where the ox stands in a neutral place, where Sumchus would require division. This entirely resolves Tosafot's question. Why, then, would Tosafot force any strained answer that undermines Rashbam when such a straightforward answer is available? This suggests at first glance that Tosafot do not hold that seizure must occur before the parties stand in beit din. Perhaps seizure afterward also helps. Then one can say that at the time of judgment the tortfeasor's ox was in the tortfeasor's house, and only afterward did the injured party seize it. Sumchus could then agree at the first stage that the burden of proof rests upon the claimant, while the later seizure addresses Rabbah bar Natan's rule. Yet we find no authority who explicitly disagrees regarding the requirement that seizure precede the litigation. In particular, the Rosh states the requirement without qualification, and Tosafot ordinarily would not disagree with him without the Rosh mentioning their position. It therefore appears that the Rosh holds as follows. Even if the claimant later says, "I did not intend to admit anything," we disregard that subjective intention because unexpressed thoughts have no legal effect. Rather, beit din itself is uncertain whether the claimant's original formulation constitutes a complete admission that exempts the defendant from the barley or whether it does not. Because this is only a slight doubt and the language leans toward admission and waiver, the claimant must satisfy two conditions in order for seizure to prevail. First, he must have seized before the doubt arose in beit din, meaning before he made the relevant claim there. Second, the seizure must have been lawful, as the Rosh writes in Bechorot in the name of Ramban, that seizure must be with permission. That means that the possessor must have had a right to seize the very item based on the claim he was asserting, as Terumat HaDeshen explains. I discussed this principle at length above in the treatise on seizure. Therefore, the claimant must have some legitimate claim concerning both items, so that his seizure is lawful. Where, according to his own position, he has no claim at all to one of the items, seizure of that item was not lawful and is ineffective. This resolves the issue. Accordingly, Tosafot can also be understood. Since beit din itself is uncertain whether the claimant's words amounted to admission and waiver, Sumchus would require division because Sumchus applies his division rule to a doubt that exists for beit din, just as in the case of whether an intercalated month belongs to the renter or the owner, where the doubt is whether we follow the first expression or the last. The authorities write that the opinion requiring division there is Sumchus. See what I wrote above in the rules of seizure. If so, were the Mishnah according to Sumchus, as Tosafot ask, there would be no need to assume seizure at all. The difficulty from the baraita that says that without proof he takes according to the tortfeasor would disappear because in truth, according to Sumchus, he would not simply take according to the tortfeasor. He would take half of the amount admitted by the tortfeasor, since beit din is uncertain whether the claimant's earlier words constituted admission or waiver, and Sumchus requires division in such a doubt. The Mishnah could not simply say "exempt," because the claimant would collect half of what the tortfeasor admitted. One might object that if the disputed ox is in the tortfeasor's house, Sumchus does not require division. That is true only where the possessor makes a definite claim. Where the possessor himself is uncertain, Sumchus requires division even when the property is in his house, as Tosafot explicitly write in Bava Metzia 100 based on the Mishnah concerning the borrowed and rented animals. Here the tortfeasor cannot make a definite legal claim that the claimant's language constituted admission. The legal effect of that language is itself uncertain. Therefore Sumchus would always require division. Everything is properly explained. This approach, however, cannot explain the Rif and Rambam according to the Mechaber, who holds that seizure even after the doubt arose is effective. According to them, we must instead use the Tur's reason, namely that since the claimant had seized the barley, his failure to demand it does not constitute an admission. Where even the claimant agrees that there was only one loan, we must resort to the more strained explanation above, that seizure is treated as though he expressly stipulated that even if the loan is found to have been barley, he neither waives nor admits away his right. This matter still requires study.
